result:
Two branches share no common ancestor commit → git can't compute a merge base, refuses by default (since 2.9) to avoid accidentally gluing separate projects together.

Usual cause: `git init` + commit locally, then pull from a remote created with its own initial commit (README/license from GitHub UI). Others: wrong remote URL, history rewritten/squashed on one side, shallow clone (`--depth`) missing the shared ancestor.

Check first: `git remote -v` points at the repo you expect. Wrong repo → fix URL, don't force the merge.

Histories really should be combined:

```
git pull origin main --allow-unrelated-histories
```

(or `git merge origin/main --allow-unrelated-histories`). Resolve conflicts (typically README/.gitignore), commit, push.

Alternatives: shallow clone → `git fetch --unshallow`, then merge normally. Local repo has nothing worth keeping → re-clone the remote instead. Want linear history → `git rebase origin/main` replays your commits on top of the remote's, no flag needed.
